source.title: IronMind: Scaling Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation via Camera-Space Ego-Centric Pretraining
source.authors: Hui-Min Pan; Y. Ren; Kun-Peng Song; Si-Yang Wang; Xi-Wen Zhang; Xiao-Yun Hu; Zhuo-Xu Duan; Han-Rui Zheng; Jia-Leng Ni; Nathan Zhao; Si-Bo Ma; Zhen-Xuan Fan; Zhong-Yang Che; Da-Yang Bao; Jiacheng Wei; J. Bai; X. Yue; Xiao-Yan Guo; Chen-Yi Chen

record.tranche_reason: Extends scaling analysis to pretraining a humanoid robot manipulation policy on egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot data, reporting validation loss and downstream performance across data budgets.
record.gate_note: The paper reports validation-loss scaling, open-loop and policy-in-the-loop metrics across pretraining budgets, a human preference study, and real-robot outcomes. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows. The exact validation-loss values per budget and the per-task bars in Figure 10 are not stated in the text, so only explicit textual results are recorded.
record.test_reason: The study varies pretraining data hours (250–10,000 h) for one robot VLA policy, with architecture, recipe and robot-data mix held fixed. It reports validation loss against data scale, which bears on V5 (non-text pretraining). It also reports open-loop, rollout, human-preference and real-robot metrics across the same budgets, which bear on V6. Parameters and compute are not varied.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors say validation loss scales approximately log-linearly from 250 to 10,000 h without saturation. They say larger budgets improve open-loop, rollout and real-robot performance, with 55.0% OOD success at 10,000 h versus at most 11.7% up to 5,000 h and 5.0% without pretraining. They acknowledge that smaller budgets are low and non-monotonic on the real robot. They frame the results as support for camera-space egocentric pretraining as a scalable foundation, and also report that camera-space beats the torso-frame baseline (55.0% vs 26.7%).
record.recipe_differences: The study varies pretraining data hours for a robot VLA policy and measures validation loss and manipulation performance; it does not test language-model loss against parameter count, token count, or training compute, nor compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: The scaling study holds architecture, optimization recipe, and heterogeneous robot-data mixture fixed while adding human-video experience. Real-robot OOD success is non-monotonic at smaller budgets and differs by task.
record.problems: The scaling study covers one architecture and one data mixture. The paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the reported scaling results. Real-robot evaluation covers one embodiment, six OOD tasks, and 10 trials per task; lower-budget results are described as low and non-monotonic.
record.rows_left_out: The exact validation-loss values at individual budgets and the remaining per-task success bars in Figure 10 are not stated in the text; they were not transcribed from the plots. No reported numeric table results relevant to V6 were otherwise omitted.

untested.parts: All of it: no language models, and parameters and compute are not varied.
No fit on small runs is used to predict larger runs.
No compute-optimal allocation of parameters versus data.
No variation of shape at a fixed parameter count.

Only data hours are varied, for one architecture and one mixture. Model-size and compute scaling are untested. The fitted form is log-linear (loss linear in log hours), not a power law, and no power-law fit is compared against it. The range is about 1.6 decades. Fine-tuning and transfer loss scaling are not measured.
Downstream performance is not predicted from pretraining loss, and no fitted downstream scaling curve is given. Model size is not varied.
Fitting choices, schedules, parameter counting and data mixtures are not varied.

missing.what: Best validation loss per budget, readable from the Figure 7(b) labels: 0.654, 0.644, 0.594, 0.580, 0.565 (the mapping to the five budgets is implied by order). Also the note that the 250 h and 500 h runs overfit during training, which is relevant to data being the bottleneck.
Per-task real-robot success and progress at each budget (0–10,000 h), shown only as bars. The text states that 10,000 h gives 40–90% per task and that gains are weaker on the Affordance tasks.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The scaling form is log-linear in data hours, which over 1.6 decades cannot be distinguished from a small-exponent power law; the study does not attempt that distinction. Real-robot scaling runs use no world-prior supervision. No uncertainty estimates are given, and real-robot results rest on 10 trials per task. The rows on Table 4 (world-prior ablation) and Table 5 (representation ablation and the InternVLA-A1.5 comparison) are correctly excluded; they are not scaling results.

versions.untested_parts: The study is about a robot manipulation policy, not language models, and does not vary parameter count, tokens, or compute to test their relationship with held-out pretraining loss.
It does not report fitting on small runs and predicting loss on runs orders of magnitude larger.
It does not compare parameter/token allocations under fixed compute budgets.
It does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Tests validation loss across pretraining data hours for one architecture and data mixture; does not test other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning loss scaling, or transfer-loss scaling.
Tests several manipulation metrics and real-robot performance against pretraining-data budget; does not test a broad range of downstream tasks or predict downstream performance from pretraining loss.
Does not vary fitting methods, parameter-counting choices, training schedules, or data mixtures to test whether exponents or curves depend on those choices.

relationships.condition: IronMind robot-VLA validation loss, 250–10,000 data hours, architecture, recipe and robot mix fixed
relationships.reason: Loss falls smoothly at −0.058 per decade with no saturation through 10,000 h (r1). The form fitted is semi-log over about 1.6 decades, not an explicit power law.
relationships.display_finding: Validation loss decreases by 0.058 per decade through 10,000 hours without saturation, following a semi-log fit over about 1.6 decades rather than an explicit power law.

relationships.condition: Open-loop and policy-in-the-loop approach metrics, human preference, and real-robot success at the largest budget
relationships.reason: 10,000 h is best on all open-loop and rollout metrics (r6, r11). Rollouts improve in order through 2,000 h (r8, r9). Raters prefer 10,000 h at 67.1% (r12). Real-robot success reaches 55.0% and rises on example tasks (r14, r17, r19).
relationships.display_finding: The 10,000-hour model led all open-loop and rollout metrics, received 67.1% human preference and reached 55.0% robot success; rollouts improved monotonically through 2,000 hours, and example robot tasks improved with scale.

relationships.condition: Intermediate budgets (2,000–5,000 h) and real-robot OOD success at budgets up to 5,000 h
relationships.reason: Some open-loop metrics worsen at intermediate budgets (eFA at 2,000 h; θalign and eFA at 5,000 h) and rollout progress ties at 2,000 and 5,000 h (r4, r5, r10). Real-robot success stays ≤11.7% and non-monotonic until an abrupt jump at 10,000 h, so it is not smoothly predictable from smaller runs (r13, r14).
relationships.display_finding: Some open-loop metrics worsened at 2,000 or 5,000 hours and rollout progress tied across those budgets, while real-robot success stayed non-monotonic and at most 11.7% before jumping at 10,000 hours.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
